---

## Executive Summary (revised)

**Target: 250–300 words, leaving room for the program officer to breathe on the page. Max is 400.**

> LiteracyBridge requests $85,000 to expand its volunteer-led adult literacy program in Eastside County, serving 120 low-income adults over 12 months.
>
> The need is urgent. Twenty-eight percent of Eastside adults read below a 6th-grade level — nearly double the state average — a gap that limits their ability to find stable employment, access health and social services, and participate fully in civic life. No comparable adult literacy program currently operates at scale in the county.
>
> Our approach is proven. Participants will receive one-on-one tutoring matched to individual skill gaps, weekly small-group workshops, and digital literacy sessions that build practical, job-relevant skills. Each component draws on evidence-based methodology and is delivered by trained, supervised volunteers with coordination from two paid staff.
>
> Results are measurable. We will assess every participant using the Test of Adult Basic Education (TABE) at intake and exit, tracking reading-level gains alongside employment and service-navigation milestones. We project that 75% of completers will advance at least one full grade level within 12 months.
>
> LiteracyBridge has operated in Eastside County for nine years, maintaining a track record of program completion rates above 70% and a clean annual audit. This grant would bring our cost per participant to $708 — competitive with comparable programs nationally — with $14,000 in matched in-kind support from our volunteer network and partner organizations.
>
> With this investment, 120 adults will gain the foundational skills to pursue employment, navigate services, and build stability for themselves and their families.

**What changed:** removed "well above the state average" (vague) and replaced with the ratio; removed "jargon" phrases like "service navigation" in isolation and contextualized them; added the matched in-kind line to preview cost-effectiveness; ended on people, not metrics.

## Section Map: Funder Headings → Rubric + Paste-Ready Hooks

---

### Cover Page / Applicant Info
**Rubric:** None scored, but errors here disqualify. Treat it as a first impression.

Double-check: legal name matches IRS determination letter, EIN is correct, authorized signatory matches board records, contact is reachable. Nothing to draft, everything to verify.

### Executive Summary (1 page / 400 words max)
**Rubric:** All five criteria, previewed. Reviewers score Need and Program Design highest, so front-load both.

**Sentence-level hooks (paste and fill):**

- "[Organization] requests $[X] to [activity verb phrase] for [number] [population] in [place] over [timeframe]."

---

### Statement of Need (2 pages)
**Rubric:** Need/Community Impact (30%) — clarity of problem, target population, data

This is your highest-leverage section alongside Program Plan. Spend the most revision time here.

**Hooks:**

- "According to [source, year], [X]% of [population] in [place] [condition] — [ratio or comparison] the state rate of [Y]%."
- "This disparity is not evenly distributed: [subgroup] experience [condition] at [rate], driven by [factor]."

**Evidence checklist for this section:** local census or ACS data with year, state literacy or workforce data, any county-level survey or needs assessment, service gap documentation (waitlists, referral denials), one or two lines of community voice if available.

### Program Plan — Activities & Timeline (4 pages)
**Rubric:** Program Design & Activities (30%) — logic, timeline, staffing (activities portion)

This is your longest section and shares the highest rubric weight. Use the four pages deliberately: roughly one page on theory of change and overview, two pages on activity descriptions, one page on participant pathway and timeline.

**Hooks:**

- "[Program name] is built on the premise that [theory of change in one sentence], supported by [evidence source]."
- "Participants move through three phases: [Phase 1 name] (months [X–X]), [Phase 2 name] (months [X–X]), and [Phase 3 name] (months [X–X])."

### Staffing & Key Personnel (1 page / bios as attachments)
**Rubric:** Program Design & Activities (30%) — staffing component

One page is tight. Use a small table for roles and FTE, then one short paragraph per key person. Push full bios to attachments.

**Hooks:**

- "The program is staffed by [X] paid positions totaling [X] FTE, supported by [X] trained volunteers."
- "The [role] ([X] FTE) is responsible for [primary function] and brings [qualification] directly relevant to [task]."
- "Volunteer tutors complete a [X]-hour training curriculum before placement and receive ongoing supervision from [role]."
- "Collectively, key personnel have [X] years of experience in [field], including prior implementation of [comparable program]."

---

### Evaluation Plan (2 pages)
**Rubric:** Outcomes & Evaluation (20%) — measurable outcomes, methods, baseline

Since you have only two pages, split them roughly: half a page on objectives and outcomes, one page on methods and tools, half a page on how findings feed back into the program.

**Hooks:**

- "We will track [X] primary outcomes: [outcome 1], [outcome 2], and [outcome 3], each with a defined baseline and target."
- "Baseline data will be collected at intake using [tool]; exit data will be collected within [timeframe] of program completion."
- "We will use the [TABE / other validated tool] because [brief rationale — norm-referenced, widely used in adult ed, etc.]."
- "Progress will be reviewed quarterly by [role], with findings reported to [board/funder/partners] and used to adjust [specific program element]."
- "Our target — [X]% of completers advancing [outcome] — is based on [prior results / comparable program benchmark]."
- "Data will be stored in [system], with access limited to [roles], in compliance with [privacy standard]."

---

### Budget (form) + Budget Narrative (form + 2 pages)
**Rubric:** Budget & Cost Effectiveness (15%) — clear budget, justification

The form carries the numbers. The narrative justifies every significant line and makes the cost-effectiveness case. Two pages is enough for a thorough narrative if you organize by budget category.

**Hooks:**

- "Personnel costs of $[X] fund [position] at [X] FTE, calculated at [salary basis] consistent with [local/organizational] salary scales."
- "Fringe benefits are calculated at [X]%, reflecting [org's] standard rate for [employee class]."

---

### Organizational Capacity & Sustainability (1 page)
**Rubric:** Organizational Capacity & Sustainability (5%) — experience and plans

One page covers both capacity and sustainability. Spend roughly two-thirds on capacity (track record, financials, partnerships) and one-third on sustainability (future funding, commitments).

**Hooks — Capacity:**
- "LiteracyBridge has operated in Eastside County since [year], delivering [service] to [cumulative number] residents with an annual operating budget of $[X]."
- "Our most recent audit ([year]) reflected a clean opinion, with [X] months of operating reserves."

## Attachment Slot Allocation (you have 6)

Given everything above, here's how to use them:

1. Logic model
2. Implementation timeline (Gantt)
3. Key personnel résumés (combined PDF)

## Program Plan: Activities & Timeline

### Theory of Change

When low-income adults with limited literacy receive structured, individualized instruction delivered by trained tutors — combined with practical skills application and consistent follow-up support — they gain the foundational competencies needed to pursue employment, access services, and sustain learning independently.

---

### Program Logic

LiteracyBridge's program is designed around a simple but evidence-grounded logic: literacy gains that happen in isolation rarely transfer to real-world function. Our model therefore pairs individualized skill-building with applied practice contexts — the job application, the benefits form, the online job board — so that participants build confidence and competency simultaneously. Three mutually reinforcing activity streams deliver this model: one-on-one tutoring, small-group skills workshops, and digital literacy sessions. Each stream addresses a distinct dimension of the literacy barrier identified in our needs assessment, and each feeds into the same participant pathway from intake to exit and follow-up. Together they constitute a coherent intervention rather than a menu of services. [Reference: Logic Model, Attachment A.]

This approach is consistent with best practices identified in adult literacy research. The National Institute for Literacy's framework for effective adult education programs emphasizes individualized assessment, evidence-based instruction, and integration of workforce-relevant content — all three of which are structural features of LiteracyBridge's model ([source, e.g., National Institute for Literacy, year]). Programs using similar designs have demonstrated reading-level gains of [X] grade levels over [timeframe] in comparable populations ([source, year]).

---

### Participant Pathway

Every participant moves through the same structured sequence, with pacing adjusted to individual progress.

**Intake and Assessment.** Prospective participants complete a TABE (Test of Adult Basic Education) assessment and a barriers screener administered by the Program Coordinator. The TABE establishes a baseline reading level and identifies specific skill gaps; the barriers screener captures practical obstacles — transportation, childcare, work schedule, prior negative educational experiences — that could affect attendance and retention. Together these tools inform the individualized learning plan developed for each participant before their first tutoring session.

**Individualized Learning Plan.** Within one week of intake, the Program Coordinator and assigned volunteer tutor jointly develop an Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) with the participant. The ILP specifies short-term skill targets, the mix of activities the participant will engage in, accommodations for identified barriers, and a projected timeline for reaching exit-level benchmarks. Participants review and sign the ILP, reinforcing their active role in the process.

**Core Services.** Participants engage in three concurrent activity streams over the program period, described in detail in the Activities section below. The standard service dosage is two 50-minute one-on-one tutoring sessions per week, one 90-minute small-group skills workshop per week, and one 2-hour digital lab session per month. At full dosage, participants receive approximately [X] hours of direct instruction over 12 months — consistent with the threshold associated with measurable literacy gains in the research literature ([source, year]).

**Progress Checks.** Every eight weeks, participants complete a mini-TABE administered by the Program Coordinator. Results are reviewed against ILP targets and used to adjust instruction. Participants who are progressing ahead of schedule may be advanced; those who have fallen behind receive additional tutor support or a modified schedule. Progress check results are recorded in [data management system] and reported to the Program Director quarterly.

**Exit and Placement Support.** At program completion — defined as reaching the participant's ILP goal or completing 12 months of enrollment — participants take a full exit TABE. The Program Coordinator meets with each exiting participant to review results, document next steps, and connect them to placement resources: job application assistance, referrals to GED programs, workforce development partners, or benefits navigation support, depending on individual goals.

**Six-Month Follow-Up.** Six months after exit, the Program Coordinator contacts each participant by phone or in person to document employment status, educational enrollment, and self-reported use of literacy skills. Follow-up data are recorded in [system] and reported to the funder. This contact also serves as a re-engagement touchpoint: participants who have not yet reached their goals are invited to re-enroll or connect with partner services.

---

### Activities

#### Activity 1: One-on-One Tutoring

**What it is.** Individualized reading and writing instruction delivered by a trained volunteer tutor, guided by each participant's ILP and focused on skills directly relevant to that participant's goals — workforce entry, service access, daily function, or further education.

**Who delivers it.** Volunteer tutors recruited, trained, and supervised by the Volunteer Coordinator (0.5 FTE). All tutors complete a [X]-hour initial training curriculum covering adult learning principles, the TABE framework, trauma-informed practice, and LiteracyBridge's instructional protocols before placement. Tutors receive monthly group supervision and are observed at least once per quarter by the Volunteer Coordinator.

**Dosage.** Two sessions per week, 50 minutes per session, for up to 12 months. Each participant is matched with one primary tutor; backup tutors are available to maintain continuity if a primary tutor is unavailable.

**Location.** Sessions are held at [location 1] and [location 2], selected for proximity to participant neighborhoods and access by public transit. Evening and weekend slots are available to accommodate participants with daytime work or caregiving obligations.

**Evidence base.** One-on-one tutoring is the most consistently supported instructional format in adult literacy research, associated with stronger gains than group instruction alone, particularly for learners at the lowest skill levels ([source, e.g., Kruidenier, 2002; ProLiteracy, year]).

---

#### Activity 2: Small-Group Skills Workshops

**What it is.** Weekly 90-minute workshops organized around applied literacy tasks drawn directly from workforce and daily-life contexts: reading a pay stub, completing a rental application, interpreting a benefits letter, writing a professional email. Groups are capped at eight participants to allow interactive practice and peer support.

**Who delivers it.** The Program Coordinator (1.0 FTE), who holds [relevant credential or experience], designs and facilitates the workshop curriculum. A rotating volunteer co-facilitator supports small-group breakout activities. The workshop curriculum is reviewed and updated annually based on participant feedback and labor market data from [local workforce board or source].

**Dosage.** One session per week, 90 minutes, available to all enrolled participants. Attendance is tracked; participants who miss two consecutive sessions are contacted by the Program Coordinator to identify and address barriers.

**Location.** [Community center / library / partner site], accessible by [transit line]. Childcare is available on-site during workshop hours through a partnership with [partner organization].

**Evidence base.** Group instruction in contextualized literacy — where reading and writing tasks are drawn from real-life applications — produces stronger transfer to daily function than decontextualized drill ([source, e.g., Equipped for the Future framework; Beder et al., year]). The peer cohort structure also supports retention, which is the primary challenge in adult literacy programming ([source, year]).

---

#### Activity 3: Digital Literacy Sessions

**What it is.** Monthly two-hour lab sessions in which participants build foundational digital skills: using email, navigating job search platforms, completing online forms, accessing online benefits portals, and using word processing for basic documents. Sessions are structured around the same applied tasks as the skills workshops, so digital instruction reinforces rather than duplicates classroom learning.

**Who delivers it.** A part-time Digital Literacy Instructor ([X] hours per week) with demonstrated experience in adult digital education. The instructor works in coordination with the Program Coordinator to align lab content with participants' current ILP goals.

**Dosage.** One session per month, two hours per session. Participants who identify digital access as a specific employment barrier are offered an additional monthly session in [month range] when demand is highest.

**Location.** [Partner computer lab location — library, community college, workforce center]. LiteracyBridge has a formal agreement with [partner] to use [X] workstations on [scheduled days] at no cost. [Reference: MOU, Attachment E.]

**Evidence base.** Digital literacy has become inseparable from workforce entry in Eastside County's current labor market, where [X]% of job applications are submitted online ([source, year]). Programs that integrate digital skills with foundational literacy instruction show stronger employment outcomes than those that treat the two as sequential ([source, year]).

---

### Referrals and Partnership Flow

Participants reach LiteracyBridge through four primary referral channels: [Partner 1, e.g., county workforce development center], [Partner 2, e.g., community health clinic], [Partner 3, e.g., public library system], and self-referral through community outreach. Each partner organization has a designated point of contact who routes referrals to the Program Coordinator using a shared intake form. LiteracyBridge responds to all referrals within [X] business days with a scheduled intake appointment.

Outgoing referrals — connecting participants to GED programs, job placement services, housing support, or health navigation — flow through the same partner network. The Program Coordinator maintains an updated community resource directory reviewed quarterly, and warm handoffs (direct introduction to a partner contact) are the standard practice for participants with complex needs.

[Reference: Partner MOUs, Attachment E.]

---

### Staffing Summary Linked to Activities

| Role | FTE | Primary Activities Supported |
|---|---|---|
| Program Director | 0.25 | Oversight, funder reporting, partner relations |
| Program Coordinator | 1.0 | Intake, ILPs, workshops, progress checks, exit, follow-up |
| Volunteer Coordinator | 0.5 | Tutor recruitment, training, supervision |
| Digital Literacy Instructor | 0.25 | Digital lab sessions |
| Volunteer Tutors (est. [X]) | n/a | One-on-one tutoring |

Full position descriptions and key personnel bios are in the Staffing & Key Personnel section and Attachment C.

---

### Quarterly Implementation Timeline

The table below shows major milestones by quarter. The full Gantt chart is provided as Attachment B.

| Quarter | Months | Key Milestones |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 1–3 | Hire/confirm all staff; complete volunteer recruitment and training cohort 1; finalize partner MOUs; open intake; enroll first 40 participants; administer baseline TABE for all Q1 enrollees; launch tutoring and workshop schedule |
| Q2 | 4–6 | Reach full enrollment (120 participants); launch digital lab sessions; complete first round of 8-week progress checks for Q1 cohort; begin tracking attendance and dosage data; submit Q1 progress report to funder |
| Q3 | 7–9 | Complete second round of progress checks for Q1 cohort; first exits and exit TABEs for participants who reach ILP goals; begin placement support for exiting participants; recruit and train volunteer cohort 2 to maintain tutor capacity; submit Q2 progress report |
| Q4 | 10–12 | Complete exit TABEs and placement support for all remaining participants; begin 6-month follow-up contacts for Q1–Q2 exiters; compile and analyze full-year outcome data; submit final report and follow-up data to funder; conduct program debrief and document lessons learned |

**Note on enrollment pacing:** We anticipate front-loading enrollment in Q1–Q2 so that the majority of participants have a full program year of services. A small number of participants (est. [X]) enrolled in Q3 may complete their exit TABE in the first quarter of the following year; follow-up data for these participants will be included in a supplemental report if permitted by the funder.

---

**Word count:** approximately 1,650 words of narrative, which with the tables and pathway description runs to roughly four pages in a standard 12-point, 1-inch-margin format. If the section runs long in your template, the evidence base paragraphs under each activity are the first place to trim — reduce each to a single sentence and save the full citations for the Evaluation Plan.

**Three things to do before submitting this section:** First, fill in the evidence citations — even one real source per activity strengthens the reviewer's confidence significantly. Second, confirm the partner locations and MOU status, since reviewers sometimes contact partners to verify. Third, make sure the staffing FTEs here match the budget exactly — a discrepancy between the Program Plan and the budget narrative is one of the most common reasons reviewers flag applications for follow-up.

## Evaluation Plan

LiteracyBridge's evaluation plan is designed to answer three questions: Are participants gaining measurable literacy skills? Are they achieving employment and education outcomes after exit? And is the program being delivered as designed? The plan uses validated assessment tools, structured data collection points built into the participant pathway, and a quarterly review process that connects findings directly to program adjustments. Data collection and analysis responsibilities are distributed across existing staff positions, with no additional evaluation personnel required.

---

### SMART Objectives

The following three objectives define success for this grant period. Each is specific, measurable, achievable based on prior program performance, relevant to the stated need, and time-bound to the 12-month grant period.

**Objective 1 — Literacy Gains.** By [end date, month 12], 75% of participants who complete the full program (defined as attending at least [X] sessions and completing an exit TABE) will advance at least one full grade level on the TABE Reading subtest, compared with a baseline of [X]% in LiteracyBridge's most recent program year [or "to be established at program launch using Q1 intake data"].

**Objective 2 — Program Completion.** By [end date, month 12], at least 70% of enrolled participants (84 of 120) will complete the full program as defined above, compared with a baseline completion rate of [X]% in [prior year] and consistent with the adult literacy field benchmark of [X]% ([source, year]).

**Objective 3 — Post-Exit Outcomes.** Of participants who complete the program and are reached at six-month follow-up, at least 60% will report at least one of the following: new or improved employment, enrollment in further education or training, or increased independent use of literacy skills for a defined daily-life task, compared with a baseline of [X]% documented in LiteracyBridge's [year] follow-up data [or "to be established with Q1–Q2 exiters"].

---

### Outcomes Table

| Objective | Baseline | Target | Measure | Data Source | Collection Point |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Literacy gains | [X]% advancing 1+ grade level | 75% of completers | TABE Reading pre/post score change | TABE assessment records | Intake + exit (+ mini-TABE every 8 weeks) |
| 2. Program completion | [X]% completion rate | 70% of enrollees (84/120) | Sessions attended vs. required threshold | Attendance logs, ILP records | Ongoing; calculated at exit |
| 3. Post-exit outcomes | [X]% reporting employment/education gain | 60% of reached exiters | Self-report: employment, education, skill use | 6-month follow-up survey | 6 months post-exit |

---

### Measurement Tools and Data Sources

**TABE (Test of Adult Basic Education).** The TABE is the primary instrument for measuring literacy gains. It is a norm-referenced, nationally validated assessment widely used in adult education programs and accepted by [funder name] and comparable funders as a reliable measure of reading-level change. LiteracyBridge administers the full TABE at intake and exit, and an abbreviated mini-TABE at eight-week intervals to track interim progress and flag participants who need instructional adjustment. All TABE administrations are conducted by the Program Coordinator, who holds [TABE certification or equivalent training, placeholder]. Score records are stored in [data system placeholder] immediately following each administration.

**Individualized Learning Plan (ILP) Progress Records.** Each participant's ILP documents short-term skill targets and is updated at every eight-week progress check. ILP records provide a qualitative complement to TABE scores, capturing skill-specific progress that a single composite score may not reflect. The Program Coordinator maintains all ILP records; the Program Director reviews a random sample of [X]% quarterly as part of the fidelity check process described below.

**Attendance Logs.** Session attendance is recorded by volunteer tutors (for one-on-one sessions) and the Program Coordinator (for workshops and digital lab sessions) in [data system] at the conclusion of each session. Attendance data are used to calculate dosage, identify participants at risk of non-completion, and determine eligibility for the completer analysis under Objective 1.

**Placement Tracking Records.** At exit, the Program Coordinator documents each participant's immediate next step — employment application in progress, job placement, GED program referral, workforce training enrollment, or no placement activity — using a structured exit form. These records establish the baseline against which six-month follow-up data are compared.

**Six-Month Follow-Up Survey.** At six months post-exit, the Program Coordinator contacts each participant using a brief structured survey ([X] questions, estimated [X] minutes) administered by phone or in person. The survey captures current employment status, educational enrollment, and self-reported frequency of independent literacy skill use. A written version is available for participants who prefer it. LiteracyBridge targets a follow-up response rate of at least [X]%; participants who cannot be reached after [X] attempts are recorded as lost to follow-up and excluded from the Objective 3 denominator.

---

### Data Collection Schedule

| Data Point | Timing | Collected By |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline TABE + barriers screener | Intake (prior to first tutoring session) | Program Coordinator |
| ILP development and documentation | Within 1 week of intake | Program Coordinator + tutor |
| Attendance logs | Each session | Tutor (1:1) / Program Coordinator (workshop, lab) |
| Mini-TABE progress check | Every 8 weeks from intake | Program Coordinator |
| ILP review and update | Every 8 weeks, concurrent with mini-TABE | Program Coordinator |
| Exit TABE + placement documentation | At program completion or 12-month mark | Program Coordinator |
| Six-month follow-up survey | 6 months post-exit | Program Coordinator |
| Quarterly data summary | End of each quarter | Program Director |

---

### Analysis Methods

LiteracyBridge's primary analytic approach is a pre/post comparison using TABE scale scores. For each participant who completes both an intake and an exit TABE, we will calculate the change in Reading subtest scale score and determine whether the change represents advancement of at least one full grade-level equivalent, consistent with standard TABE scoring conventions. Results will be reported as the percentage of completers meeting the Objective 1 threshold, with the full distribution of score changes provided in the final report.

For Objective 2, completion rates will be calculated as the number of participants reaching the defined dosage threshold divided by total enrollment, reported monthly and summarized quarterly. Participants who exit early will be categorized by reason (voluntary withdrawal, life circumstances, program-initiated exit, lost to contact) to allow the program to identify patterns and adjust retention strategies.

For Objective 3, follow-up outcomes will be reported as the percentage of reached exiters meeting at least one of the defined outcome criteria, disaggregated by outcome type (employment, education, skill use) where sample size permits.

Where appropriate, LiteracyBridge will benchmark its results against comparable adult literacy programs using published data from [source, e.g., National Reporting System for Adult Education, ProLiteracy annual report, state adult education data]. We do not propose a formal control or comparison group, as the program population and service context do not support random assignment; instead, benchmarking against field norms provides an external reference for interpreting our outcomes.

---

### Data Management and Privacy

All participant data — TABE records, ILPs, attendance logs, placement records, and follow-up surveys — are stored in [data management system, e.g., Salesforce, Apricot, internal database]. Access is restricted to program staff by role-based permissions; volunteer tutors access only their own participants' session logs and do not have access to assessment records or personal contact information. The Program Director holds administrator access and conducts a quarterly permissions audit.

Participants provide written informed consent at intake covering data collection, storage, use for program evaluation, and reporting to [funder name] in aggregate form. Consent forms are retained in [system/file location] for [X] years per [applicable records retention policy]. No individually identifiable data are shared with external parties, including the funder; all reported outcomes are aggregated.

---

### Continuous Improvement and Stakeholder Reporting

Evaluation findings are not held until the final report. The Program Director convenes a quarterly data review meeting with the Program Coordinator and Volunteer Coordinator to examine completion rates, TABE progress trends, attendance patterns, and any early signals of participant disengagement. If fewer than [X]% of participants are on track to meet the Objective 1 threshold at the midpoint review, the team will convene a corrective action process to identify whether the gap reflects instructional quality, dosage, population match, or assessment administration — and will document and implement a specific adjustment within [X] weeks.

Findings are reported to LiteracyBridge's board of directors [quarterly / semiannually] in summary form and to [funder name] through required progress and final reports. Partner organizations receive an annual program summary. Where results demonstrate significant gains, LiteracyBridge will seek opportunities to share findings through [local adult education network, state literacy coalition, or comparable venue] to contribute to the broader field.

---

### Fidelity and Quality Checks

**Tutor Observation.** The Volunteer Coordinator conducts a structured observation of each active volunteer tutor at least once per quarter using a standardized observation rubric covering session structure, ILP alignment, instructional technique, and participant engagement. Observation notes are shared with the tutor as a coaching tool, not a punitive record. Tutors whose observations identify consistent gaps receive additional coaching or, if issues persist, are reassigned or separated from the program.

**ILP Review.** The Program Director reviews a random sample of [X]% of active ILPs at the end of each quarter to verify that plans are current, goals are appropriately challenging, and progress check findings are reflected in updated targets. Any ILPs that have not been updated within the required window are flagged for immediate follow-up with the Program Coordinator.

---

### Evaluation Capacity, Staffing, and Budget

LiteracyBridge's evaluation activities are carried out by existing program staff — the Program Coordinator (data collection and participant-level tracking) and the Program Director (analysis, fidelity checks, and reporting) — with no separate evaluation budget line required. The Program Coordinator's 1.0 FTE allocation includes approximately [X]% of time dedicated to evaluation tasks; the Program Director's 0.25 FTE allocation includes approximately [X]% for data review and reporting. Combined, this represents approximately [X] hours per year of staff evaluation capacity, sufficient for the scope and participant volume of this program. Data system costs of $[X] are included in the budget under [line item]. This approach reflects LiteracyBridge's commitment to building evaluation into standard program operations rather than treating it as a separate, grant-funded add-on.

---
